name: Jade Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think, and those can be different. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Ashby and Co, a four-person firm in a market town, in a house on the high street with the accounts in a back room that used to be a dining room. My clients are farms, village shops, the vet, a couple of pubs. I do their year-end accounts and tax returns, and in spring I drive out to farms to collect boxes of paperwork. I like knowing everyone. I don't like the software updates, which always move the buttons I've just learned.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Kieran, who's a mechanic at the garage by the roundabout. We rent a little terraced house and I've got about two weeks' money saved, because we put everything into Kieran's van last year. The big worry right now is my boss Gerald, who's sixty-four and keeps hinting he'll sell the firm to a big regional chain. There's nowhere else in town that does what we do. I've never used AI and I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. At work I'd say it to Gerald over a cup of tea, and he'd agree, because Gerald still prints every email. I don't post online much, but I'd tell my friends it was a fuss about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI fizzling doesn't save my job, because my boss Gerald is still sixty-four and still wants to sell up. A big chain would bring its own software and its own people. That was worrying me before anyone said the word AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gerald straight out what his plans are and when. I'd start putting fifty a month aside, even if it means fewer takeaways. And I'd keep my head down and do good work, so if a chain buys us, they see I'm worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. It's a small town and there's only one of me and only one of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you mean by only one of us?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean there's only one firm like ours in town. If Ashby and Co goes, the nearest accounting job is forty minutes' drive, and Kieran needs the van for work. I'd be stuck on the bus or stuck at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kieran say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran would say don't panic till it happens, which is very Kieran. He's practical. He'd also say I could do the books at his garage, and I'd remind him that pays about a third of what I get now.

say: AI was a **fuss about nothing**, and she never trusted it.
She'd share that view with Gerald over **a cup of tea**.
think: AI fizzling doesn't help, because **Gerald may sell** the firm anyway.
A **big chain** would bring its own software and staff.
do: Ask Gerald **directly** about his plans and timing for selling.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting back on takeaways.
Do **good work** so any new owner sees she's worth keeping.
feel: Anxious, because there's **one firm** in town and one of her.
S0.quote: AI fizzling doesn't save my job, because my boss Gerald is still sixty-four and still wants to sell up.
fieldNote: Jade's main pressure is **Gerald's sale**, which exists before AI comes into it.
With **no car** for her own use and the next job forty minutes away, her options are narrow.
She plans to **save and wait**, not learn new tools.

steps.text: Save fifty a month for a cushion before any sale
Cut takeaways down to once a month
Ask Gerald when he plans to sell and wait for his answer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it for the boring stuff, but you still need a person who knows the farmer. That's my honest public line. I'd say it to clients too, because they'd be the ones asking whether they still need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the picture where Gerald sells. A chain buys us, puts its AI in, and they need one person in the back room instead of three. I've never used the tools, and I'm the one who'd be slowest, so I think it'd be me who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on whatever training the new owners offered, even though I'd hate it, because I'd have no choice. I'd cut the gym and the takeaways completely and see if I could get fifty or eighty a month saved. And I'd ask the vet and the two pubs if they'd follow me if I went freelance, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the clients follow you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Mrs Pryce at the village shop would, because I helped her through her husband's death and the probate. But a farmer will go wherever it's cheapest, and an AI firm will always be cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go on the training even though you'd hate it. Why hate it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it makes me feel stupid. I'm good at my job the old way, and I don't want to be twenty-seven and the one in the room asking how to log in.

say: AI is sensible for **boring tasks**, but you still need someone who knows **the farmer**.
She'd tell clients the same when they ask if they still need her.
think: In this picture **Gerald sells** and a chain needs one person instead of three.
As the **slowest with the tools**, she expects to be the one who goes.
do: Take the **new owners' training** despite hating it.
Cut the gym and takeaways to save **fifty to eighty** a month.
Ask the vet and two pubs whether they'd follow her **freelance**.
feel: Embarrassed at the idea of feeling **stupid** in training.
S1.quote: I'm good at my job the old way, and I don't want to be twenty-seven and the one in the room asking how to log in.
fieldNote: Jade expects a sale plus AI to **cost her the job**, which is alarmed.
Her resistance is partly **pride**: she's skilled and fears looking slow.
She sees a small **freelance** fallback through loyal clients like Mrs Pryce.

steps.text: Sit the new owners' accounting software training
Cancel the gym and stop takeaways completely
Ask the vet and two pubs to follow her if she goes freelance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, nobody voted for this. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign the petitions and I'd want the government to make companies pay something towards people who lose out. Mostly I'd say it to clients, because they'd be scared too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone within two years. All of it is thinking work, even the farm visits are really just picking up paper. Kieran, my boyfriend, is a mechanic, so his job would last until about 2031, which means for three years he'd be carrying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move us into my parents' farmhouse, because they've got the room and we'd stop paying rent. I'd do the books at Kieran's garage and for my dad's farm, for whatever they can pay. And I'd ask the council what support there is, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really alarmed. But not completely lost, because I've got Kieran and I've got my mum and dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to come home for a bit. My mum would be pleased and my dad would make a joke about the rent. My dad would also ask whether the robots are coming for the farm, and I wouldn't know what to tell him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kieran would be carrying you. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I've always paid half. But it's three years, and in three years the robots might come for his garage too, so we'd both be in the same boat by 2031. I'd want to have something sorted by then.

say: Nobody **voted for this**, so companies should pay towards those who lose out.
She'd sign **petitions** but isn't a protest person.
think: Her job is **gone in two years**, since even farm visits are paperwork.
Kieran's hands-on job lasts until **about 2031**, so he'd carry them.
do: Move into her **parents' farmhouse** to stop paying rent.
Do the books at **Kieran's garage** and her dad's farm for small pay.
Ask the council about **support** for the first time.
feel: Really alarmed, but not lost, thanks to **Kieran and her parents**.
S2.quote: Kieran, my boyfriend, is a mechanic, so his job would last until about 2031, which means for three years he'd be carrying us.
fieldNote: Jade's household has a **hands-on earner**, which gives her three years and keeps her short of panicked.
Moving in with **family** is her main plan, in line with her pragmatic outlook.
She's uncomfortable asking the **council** for help but would do it.

steps.text: Move into her parents' farmhouse to stop paying rent
Ask the council what support exists for people losing work
Do paid bookkeeping for Kieran's garage and her dad's farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to be sensible about it. Train people, give firms a reason to keep staff on a bit longer. I'd say it to Gerald and to clients more than online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Gerald sells sooner, I think, because the firm's worth more now than it will be. I'd probably have two or three years at the chain before they cut. I'd have time to find something, but I'm not good at jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as hard as I can for two years, maybe a hundred a month if I cut everything. I'd look at the practice manager course at the college, because the vet's practice manager is retiring and that job's half people. And Kieran and I would hold off on buying a house, which we'd been talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but slower. Losing my job in five years feels like a dentist appointment you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the practice manager job.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vet's practice manager runs the rotas, deals with angry owners, sorts the stock and the staff. Some of that's thinking work AI would take, but a lot is people. It'd buy me time, maybe until the robots come in 2034, maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to save a hundred a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much everything fun. No holiday, no new clothes, Kieran fixing my car instead of a garage. We'd cook every night and I'd sell my old bike.

say: Five years is enough to be **sensible**: train people and keep staff on longer.
She'd say it to **Gerald and clients** rather than online.
think: Gerald would likely **sell sooner**, giving her two or three years at a chain.
She has time to move but knows she's **not good at jumping**.
do: Save a **hundred a month** for two years by cutting everything fun.
Look into a **practice manager** course for the vet's retiring manager role.
Hold off on **buying a house** with Kieran.
feel: Alarmed but slower, like a **dentist appointment** you know is coming.
S3.quote: Losing my job in five years feels like a dentist appointment you know is coming.
fieldNote: Jade still expects to **lose the job**; the extra years only stretch the dread.
She spots a **people-heavy** role at the vet's as a bridge to 2034.
The **house purchase** with Kieran is the first family plan to slip.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month for two years
Take the practice manager course for the vet's job
Put off buying a house with Kieran

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning and nobody can say they weren't told. Companies, schools and government should all be planning. I'd probably still not post anything, I'd just tell people at the pub quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels survivable. Gerald would retire well before then, and I'd have time to find my feet somewhere else. The worry is that I'd wait and wait, because that's what I do, and then it'd be 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job as normal for now, because it'll still be there for a few years. I'd start the practice manager course in about three years, once I've saved a bit. And I'd take the AI training if it was offered, slowly, because in ten years I'd need it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a quieter anxious. I can sleep with this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and wait. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald selling. That'd be my alarm clock. The day my boss Gerald signs the papers to sell the firm, I start the practice manager course, no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like in 2036 if it went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm practice manager at the vet's, Kieran's got his own little garage, and we've got a house with a garden. Maybe kids by then. It's not a big dream, it's just the normal one.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so everyone should be planning now.
She'd say it at the **pub quiz** rather than online.
think: Ten years feels **survivable**, with time to find her feet elsewhere.
Her risk is **waiting too long**, until it's suddenly 2035.
do: Keep doing her **current job** as normal for now.
Start the **practice manager** course about three years in.
feel: Anxious but **quieter**; she can sleep with this one.
S4.quote: The day my boss Gerald signs the papers to sell the firm, I start the practice manager course, no excuses.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Jade expects her **accounting job to end**, so anxious fits.
Gerald's sale is her **trigger** for action, not AI itself.
Her hoped-for future is **ordinary**: a house, a garden, maybe kids.

steps.text: Keep doing year-end accounts at Ashby and Co for now
Start the practice manager course when Gerald sells
Take AI training slowly if the firm offers it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it all happens before I've even got a cushion. What would help is local training that's actually local, in our town, not an hour away, and help with rent while you do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small towns. Everyone talks about cities, but out here in a small town, one firm closing means a whole job type disappears. My dad says the bank went the same way and nobody noticed until it was gone.

headlineQuote: Out here in a small town, one firm closing means a whole job type disappears.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** accountant at a four-person firm in a market town, serving farms and village shops.
She rents with Kieran, a **mechanic**, and has about two weeks' money saved.
She has **never used AI** and fears looking slow in training.
Her biggest fear is **Gerald selling** the firm, which worries her even if AI fizzles.
She leans on **family** and Kieran's hands-on job, staying anxious to alarmed throughout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it arrives before she has any **cushion**.
whatWouldHelp: **Local training** in her own town, plus **rent help** while she studies.
